## Nobody reads the logs until something burns

Three in the morning. Checkout is failing for maybe one in forty customers, and the dashboard is green.

That gap — between a system that looks fine and a system that is fine — is the whole argument for observability, and most teams only feel it during an incident, when the cost of learning is highest.

Monitoring answers questions you thought to ask in advance. You picked the metrics, set the thresholds, wired the pages. It works right up until the failure is something nobody predicted, which, for any service with more than a handful of moving parts, is most failures. A p99 latency graph will not tell you that the slow requests all come from one tenant whose account has 400,000 rows in a table you assumed held ten.

Observability is the ability to ask a new question of a running system without shipping new code to answer it. In practice that means traces that carry request context across service boundaries, structured events rich enough to slice by customer or region or build SHA, and logs someone can actually search.

The payoff is not shorter incidents, though incidents do get shorter. It is that engineers stop guessing. Debugging turns from an argument about whose service is at fault into a query, and the person running that query is often whoever shipped the code last week, not the one who has been here six years and remembers where the bodies are.

---

## Why Observability Matters

The checkout page is slow. That's all the ticket says.

So you start guessing. Maybe it's the database. Someone pulls up a dashboard showing CPU at 40%, which tells you nothing. Someone else remembers a deploy on Thursday and starts scrolling through the diff. An hour in, three engineers are working from three different theories, and nobody can prove any of them wrong. Eventually the graph flattens out on its own and everyone goes back to what they were doing, quietly hoping it doesn't come back.

It comes back.

This is what it feels like to operate a system you can't see into. Monitoring told you *that* something was wrong: a threshold was crossed, an alert fired, a pager went off. It didn't tell you why, and it couldn't, because you have to know a failure mode in advance to write an alert for it. Most of the failures that actually hurt you are the ones nobody predicted.

Observability is the difference between watching a system and being able to interrogate it. It means that when the checkout page gets slow, you can ask a question you never anticipated asking — which customers, on which plan, hitting which downstream service, holding which feature flag — and get an answer in the time it takes to type it. Not from a dashboard someone built last quarter. From the data itself.

That capability changes more than incident response. It changes what your team is willing to build, ship, and change. The rest of this post is about how.

**What a year of remote work actually taught us**

We went fully remote in March and spent the first two months congratulating ourselves. Commute time gone. Office lease gone. Two engineers moved somewhere with cheaper rent and stayed.

Then the cracks showed up, and none of them were the ones we'd braced for.

Productivity was fine. It was never the problem. What broke was the stuff that used to happen by accident: the half-question you'd ask someone walking past their desk, the sense that a project was going sideways before anyone wrote it down. On Slack, nobody asks a half-question. They wait until it's a whole one, which usually means waiting three days.

So we started writing more. Design docs before code, weekly written updates instead of standups. It felt bureaucratic for about six weeks and then it felt normal. The unexpected benefit was that new hires could read a year of decisions instead of asking someone to recount them badly from memory.

The other thing we got wrong: we assumed everyone wanted this. Two people were miserable. One lived alone in a studio apartment and hadn't spoken aloud in four days when he told us. We now cover coworking space for anyone who wants it, no explanation required. Six people take it.

Meetings dropped by roughly half. The half that survived are longer and better attended.

If we'd known one thing going in, it's that remote work doesn't remove overhead. It moves it into writing, where it's slower to produce and much cheaper to reuse.

## Technical Debt

Nobody plans to take on technical debt. It shows up anyway — in the Friday hotfix that never got a second pass, in the config flag someone added for one customer in 2021 and everybody has been too polite to remove since.

The metaphor gets abused. Debt implies you borrowed something on purpose and know the terms, and most of what we call debt is closer to sediment: it settled. Nobody signed for it. There's no interest rate you can look up, only the growing sense that a change which used to take a day now takes a week, and nobody can say exactly when that happened.

This issue is about getting specific. Three teams walk through a system they were afraid of, what it actually cost them to keep it, and what they did about it — including one case where the answer was to leave it alone and write down why.

We're not going to tell you to allocate 20% of every sprint to cleanup. You've read that advice. It doesn't survive contact with a launch date. What we do have is a handful of engineers describing, concretely, how they made the argument to ship less this quarter and won.

**The Interest Payment**

Nobody schedules technical debt. It arrives the way most debt does: one reasonable decision at a time, each defensible on the day it was made. The hardcoded config that shipped a demo on Friday. We've been talking about it a lot lately, mostly because of a rule we started following in April: when a ticket takes three times longer than anyone guessed, we write down why. Six months of those notes make a pattern hard to ignore. It's rarely the hard problems that eat the schedule. It's the six-year-old service nobody wants to open.

So this month we're printing the notes. Rina walks through the payments refactor and is honest about what it cost. Dev writes about the parts of our test suite that exist only to pass. Two teams disagree, in print, about whether the scheduler is worth rewriting or worth deleting.

# Managed Database vs. Self-Hosted

The trade is money for attention. A managed service (RDS, Cloud SQL, Neon, PlanetScale) charges roughly two to four times the raw compute cost, and in exchange takes over the work that wakes people at 3 a.m.: failover, backups, patching, replica promotion. Running it yourself costs less per gigabyte and more per engineer.

**What you actually get.** Automated backups with tested point-in-time recovery. Failover that has been exercised on someone else's fleet, not just in your runbook. Minor-version patching on a schedule you can defer but not ignore.

**What you give up.** Superuser. No custom extensions outside the provider's list, no kernel tuning, no `pg_stat_statements` variants they haven't blessed. Connection limits are set by instance class, so you may need PgBouncer anyway. And your storage layer becomes a black box: when p99 latency doubles, you file a ticket instead of reading `iostat`.

**Cost crossover.** Managed wins until you're spending five figures a month, at which point a dedicated DBA becomes cheaper than the markup. Egress fees and cross-AZ replication traffic are where the bill surprises people.

**A decision rule.** Self-host if you have someone on staff who has restored a production database from backup under time pressure, and you need control the provider won't give you. Otherwise use managed, and spend the saved headcount on your application.

Migration between the two is not symmetric. Moving onto a managed service is a dump and restore. Moving off means rebuilding the operational muscle you stopped using.

# Managed database or self-hosted?

The decision usually reduces to what your team's time is worth and how far into the engine you need to reach.

**What managed buys.** RDS, Cloud SQL, Neon and their peers handle backups, failover, minor-version patching, and the 3 a.m. page. Adding a replica is an API call. For a five-person team shipping product, that's the whole argument.

**What self-hosting buys.** Control of the version, the extensions, the page cache, the disk layout. Cost that stays predictable as you grow: past a few hundred gigabytes at steady traffic, the spread gets hard to ignore. You can pin an old version indefinitely and colocate the database with the app to drop a network hop.

**What self-hosting costs.** Someone owns backups and has actually restored one. Someone owns failover and has watched it fire. That's a standing fraction of an engineer, plus enough rotation depth to survive vacations. The work doesn't scale down — a small deployment needs nearly the same discipline as a large one.

**Rough rule.** Under ~500 GB, or with no dedicated infra person: go managed. Above that, with the staff and a concrete reason to tune, self-hosting starts paying for itself.
